people.name: Arthur T. Packard
people.role: Editor of the Bad Lands Cow Boy; Medora stage line manager
people.bio: Arthur T. Packard was the editor of the Bad Lands Cow Boy, which he launched at Little Missouri, beside Medora, in February 1884 and marked as one year old in January 1885. In his first months he started a museum of Bad Lands curiosities at the office, became the local agent for Studebaker wagons, and fought rival Dickinson over the freight route to Deadwood. In August 1884 he went to St. Paul to close the contracts for the Medora Forwarding and Stage Company, and in September the paper called him the stage line's general manager as he left for Pierre as a delegate to the Republican territorial convention. The Cow Boy office also sold receipts for the Medora coal mine and wrote insurance, and Packard advertised barb wire for sale in 1886. His editorials took on the Custer County ring, a libelous Bismarck telegram about Medora in 1886, and the leaders of the South Dakota statehood movement, and in March 1886 he was named a judge for the Billings County election.

people.name: Marquis de Morès
people.role: Founder of Medora; president of the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co.
people.bio: The Cow Boy described the Marquis de Morès as a young Frenchman, son-in-law of the New York banker von Hoffman, who had bought large stretches of grazing land on the Little Missouri. In early 1884 he traveled to Washington about a freight and mail route to Deadwood, and that April he rode to Deadwood with Joe Pennell, making the return ride in twenty-six hours, and agreed to put on a stage line from Medora to Deadwood. He signed company notices as president, and in October 1884 ordered 200 cords of stone for a new refrigerator and received an order for 500 cattle from a Chicago firm. Alfalfa seed arrived for experiments in his garden in June 1884, and in 1885 believed he had found kaolin clay near Medora. In March 1885 the paper announced the birth of his son, and in September 1885 he stood trial at Bismarck over the killing of Luffsey, with defense witnesses testifying that Luffsey and O'Donald had threatened to shoot him on sight. In January 1886 he returned from France, and in October 1886 the paper credited him and Theodore Roosevelt, as Dakota members of the Montana Stockgrowers' Association executive committee, with quick action against a cattle disease.

people.name: Howard Eaton
people.role: Bad Lands cattleman who called the first stockmen's meeting
people.bio: Howard Eaton was one of the most frequently named cattlemen in the Cow Boy, signing the February 1884 notices that called Bad Lands stockmen together for a meeting. That spring the paper reported that two visiting lumbermen, G. F. Randall and A. J. Rich, would put 1,000 head on the range in his charge, and in June 1884 he and Lloyd Roberts drove in a thousand head for the Badger cattle company. He spent the winter of 1884-85 on an eastern trip for treatment of his leg, received three carloads of bulls in June 1885, and regularly hosted eastern visitors from Pittsburgh and Boston for hunting in the Bad Lands. In February 1886 he obtained a lawyer's opinion that the Stark County tax levied on the area was unconstitutional, and that spring he brought a Bismarck dentist to Medora for a week. In October 1886 he sold three cars of cattle in St. Paul, and in November the new Billings County commissioners paid him for election work in the county's organization.

people.name: E. G. Paddock
people.role: Medora livery stable owner, stockman and cattle buyer
people.bio: E. G. "Geary" Paddock was one of the early Little Missouri townspeople; a letter in one of the Cow Boy's first issues joked that he expected the paper to boom his town lots there. In March 1884 he sat on the five-man committee that drafted by-laws for the Bad Lands stockmen's association, and that May he, Lloyd Roberts and Dan Friedman brought 750 head of cattle from Minnesota for Rich, Randall & Co. From June 1884 into January 1885 he was among the signers of a standing $250 reward for information on anyone setting grass fires, and in late November 1884 he was elected to the school board. He won the first two Bad Lands Gun Club shoots for a rifle, in late February and early March 1885, and that spring opened a livery and sale stable in Medora that he soon planned to double in size; the April 1886 Billings County election was held in his livery office. In September 1885 the paper reported that the murder case against him and the Marquis over the killing of Luffsey had been moved to Bismarck on a change of venue, with both under arrest and bail refused, and later that month that he had been discharged. In October 1886 the paper noted him shipping cattle to St. Paul and visiting his old home at Wadena, Minn.

people.name: W. F. Van Driesche
people.role: Medora postmaster; Stage company treasurer; Billings County treasurer, 1886
people.bio: William F. Van Driesche, who signed himself Wm. F. or W. F. Van Driesche, took a place in the Medora post office in February 1884 and signed the unclaimed-letter lists that March; he signed as assistant postmaster in the fall of 1884, and as postmaster from April 1885 through late 1886. In the spring of 1884 he signed the call for the Republican county convention and won a wager with Frank Keeler that he could ride a bucking horse for half an hour. He was treasurer of the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co., signing a March 1885 notice issued with the Marquis de Morès as president. In February 1885 he was elected president and treasurer of the new gun club, and in July 1885 he took the Marquis's place on a hunting trip to the Big Horn country with the Marquise. In April 1886 he was elected Billings County treasurer, and he also sat as an election judge; he was re-elected treasurer in November 1886 but resigned in December. In August 1886, when the prairie chicken season opened, he and Frank Foster bagged thirty-three birds in less than two hours.

people.name: Bob Roberts
people.role: Medora freighter, saloon keeper and Deadwood route pioneer
people.bio: Bob Roberts was a Medora freighter and saloon keeper. In the spring of 1884 the paper reported him running mule freight outfits between Medora and Deadwood, leading the first train over the new route and cutting a shorter road to the Black Hills. That fall he served as one of Dakota's deputy commissioners for the New Orleans exposition, travelled to Bismarck on its business, and planned to start for New Orleans with Vic Smith in January 1885; late that month he left instead for Wales to settle his father's estate. The Cow Boy also noted his cellar for liquor stock, his building (where Sam Whitney set up house in April 1885), and a pet bear that amused the town. In January 1886 the firm of Roberts & Co., his partnership with James Hannigan, was dissolved, and that July his lease of a building to Billings County for county purposes was signed and filed.

people.name: Theodore Roosevelt
people.role: Rancher (Elkhorn, Maltese Cross); chairman of Little Missouri stockgrowers' association
people.bio: The future president, then a New York reformer and Bad Lands rancher, first appears in June 1884 visiting his ranch managed by Ferris & Merrifield and calling at the Cow Boy office in full cowboy dress. In December 1884 he called a meeting of Little Missouri stockmen and chaired it, and through 1886 the paper printed his notices as chairman and president of the Little Missouri River Stockmen's (later Stockgrowers') Association, whose meetings and round-ups he called. In May 1885 fifteen hundred yearlings and two-year-olds arrived for his Elkhorn and Chimney Butte ranches, and that year the paper noted his published account of a Big Horn hunt and an elk he shot down the river. In February 1886 it reported about 100 applications for jobs on his ranch after a lecture he gave on ranch life, and in April it praised his brisk handling of the stock meeting. That fall he and the Marquis de Morès guaranteed the money to kill and bury a quarantined, diseased herd, and in November he telegraphed the Ferris brothers that he had lost the election for mayor of New York.

people.name: J. N. Maxwell
people.role: Northern Pacific and express agent at Medora, 1884-86
people.bio: J. N. Maxwell came to Medora in November 1884 from the car accountant's office at Mandan, trading places with agent Fegan to become the Northern Pacific agent. In December 1884 he was also made agent for two rival express companies, including Wells, Fargo & Co. Through 1885 his name ran as agent at the foot of the Northern Pacific time table printed in the paper. In September 1885 the paper announced his marriage. In January 1886 he was to serve temporarily as Wells-Fargo agent at Billings before going to St. Paul, and by February 1886 he was an express messenger on the Jamestown Northern road between Jamestown and Minnewaukon.

people.name: J. C. Fisher
people.role: Medora businessman, postmaster, stage line manager and Republican leader
people.bio: J. C. Fisher was a Medora businessman and Republican organizer who chaired the county central committee in 1884. In August 1884 he became local manager of the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co., and that fall he built two stores on Third Avenue and talked of adding a roller rink. By January 1885 he was signing the post office's unclaimed-letter lists as postmaster, and with Rassie Deffebach he ran the roller rink, where he also kept a shooting gallery and fitted up the post office. He chaired the December 1884 school meeting, served as a school trustee in 1885, and rode out to the E6 ranch and Wadsworth's beef round-up that year. He appeared on the Stockmen's Ticket in March 1886, and in December 1886 he left to spend a month or more in Elyria, Ohio.

people.name: John W. Goodall
people.role: Round-up foreman and Billings County commissioner
people.bio: John W. (Johnny) Goodall was a Little Missouri cattleman and round-up foreman. In April 1884 the stockmen recommended him as foreman of the round-up, and that spring he brought back 47 cow horses from the west, along with the Mexican rider Perfecto Fernandez; that winter he broke teams for the stage road. In April 1885 the Montana Stock-growers' Association named him to district the Little Missouri, and in April 1886 the Little Missouri River Stockgrowers' Association elected him foreman of the spring round-up. He married in August 1885, entered horses in Medora's Fourth of July races that year, and ran for Billings County commissioner on the March 1886 ticket; by July he sat on the board and chaired meetings pro tem. He was elected commissioner for Precinct Two in November 1886, and in December left for San Antonio, Texas, on business for the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co.

people.name: Dr. H. M. Jorgens
people.role: Medora druggist and merchant from Spearfish; Cave Hills rancher
people.bio: Dr. H. M. Jorgens came from Spearfish in the Black Hills, and in May 1884 the paper reported that he and Dr. J. M. Louthan had decided to set up business in Medora. In August 1884 he promised to return with a stock of drugs, and in September he toured the Deadwood stage route with Vic Smith. A burned range kept him in Spearfish that fall while he found winter feed for his cattle, but by early 1885 he had brought his wife and sons to Medora from the Cave Hills. In April 1885 he put up a new building for his drug store, and he also sold stationery, notions, jewelry and fancy goods. In December 1885 he started a gift enterprise for customers, and when he received fresh vaccine the paper urged everyone to be vaccinated. Through 1885 and 1886 he made regular trips to Spearfish and to his Cave Hills ranch, where he hauled supplies in July 1886.

people.name: Gregor Lang
people.role: Manager of the Neimmela Ranch, Medora; cattleman on the Little Missouri
people.bio: Gregor Lang was listed among the cattlemen of the Medora district at the stockmen's meeting of March 1884, and that month the paper marveled that his herd had gone two months without water and was still fat. He had a horse stolen from the Cantonment in April 1884, which was tracked and recovered, and in June 1884 he brought in another large lot of cattle carrying his new "triangle JP" brand. From July 1884 into early 1885 he ran a $50 reward notice for three missing mares and a pony, and in the March 1885 brand directory he appeared as manager of the Neimmela Ranch, Medora. In September 1885 he satisfied the Little Missouri River Stockgrowers' Association that a disputed branding had been lawful, and in December 1885 he settled George Fitzgerald's brand case by buying Fitzgerald's brand. He was on the Billings County ticket for justice in spring 1886, one of his hands, Henry Williams, won a steer-roping prize at the June 1886 round-up, and that September he sold his cattle at St. Paul.

people.name: Fred A. Willard
people.role: Stock inspector, deputy U.S. marshal and Billings County sheriff
people.bio: Fred A. Willard came to Medora in June 1885 as the stock inspector appointed by the Montana stock association, and in July he went to Fargo for his commission as a deputy U.S. marshal. Over the next year and a half he recovered strayed horses for ranchers, posted notices against firing guns in public, took a rifle away from a drunken man in December 1885, and inspected at the slaughter-house. He was named for sheriff on the Billings County ticket in March 1886 and elected in April, and his bond as sheriff was accepted in May. In October 1886 he and John Goodall went to Oliver County to quarantine a herd believed to have pleuro-pneumonia; that month he was renominated for sheriff, and he was re-elected in November. In December 1886 he brought George Myers back to Medora on a warrant sworn out by the Montana Stockgrowers' Association.

people.name: Erasmus Deffebach
people.role: Superintendent of the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co.; later cattle foreman
people.bio: Erasmus 'Rassie' Deffebach came to Medora from Spearfish in the Black Hills in spring 1884, renting the company stable that June and moving his family to town in August. As superintendent of the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co., he bought horses at Helena in September 1884 and announced that coaches to Deadwood would start on October 6, and he signed a certificate with Arthur T. Packard that month. In early 1885 the paper reported news of a family fortune awaiting the Deffebach heirs in Germany, and he and J. C. Fisher ran Medora's roller rink. In July 1885 M. Wadsworth hired him as foreman for the Bad Lands Cattle Co., and he moved his family to Dickinson; in January 1886 he went to the E6 camp.

people.name: J. L. Truscott
people.role: Rancher; secretary of stockmen's association; chairman of Billings County commissioners
people.bio: J. L. Truscott was a Little Missouri cattleman who took part in the Bad Lands stockmen's meeting of March 1884 and came in from Beaver creek at the close of the district's first round-up that June. He was among the ranchers who called a stockmen's meeting in December 1884, and in spring 1885 he was elected secretary of the Little Missouri River Stockgrowers' Association. In July 1885 his bride, the former Maggie Gardient, arrived in Medora, and in December 1885 the paper reported the birth of a daughter at the Spring creek ranch. Elected a Billings County commissioner in 1886, he was chosen chairman of the board in May and presided over meetings on liquor licenses and county bills. In August 1886 the stockgrowers named him to represent them at Bismarck if cattle legislation was needed, and that fall he was nominated again for commissioner.

people.name: Joseph A. Ferris
people.bio: Joseph A. Ferris was a Medora merchant who in February 1884 reported his cattle wintering without loss and in March went to Mandan to buy dry goods for a new store. Through 1884 he added groceries, a new store room across the river and a warehouse for his stock. In June 1885 he began a two-story store building on Main Street, opened it with a house-warming dance in early August, and moved his goods in that month; the paper also reported a building put up for Mrs. Malloy on one of his lots. He married in New Brunswick in January 1886, was named for probate judge on the Stockmen's Ticket that March but withdrew, became Medora's sole agent for Collins' goods in April, and in June sued Mrs. P. Malloy for possession of property.

people.name: Talleyrand Martin
people.role: Medora druggist, weather observer and Billings County coroner
people.bio: Talleyrand Martin ran the Medora drug store with Dr. Jorgens from late 1884 and kept the town's weather record, which the Cow Boy printed regularly from December 1884. In April 1885 he was collecting Bad Lands petrified specimens, and the drug store moved into what the paper called the best store room in town. In May 1885 the paper began running his report weekly, and he sent six months of observations to Gen. W. B. Hazen, chief of the weather bureau, who added him to its volunteer contributors. He was elected Billings County coroner in April 1886, served as a judge at the election organizing Medora's school township, and in September 1886 published a detailed report on a July heat the paper called remarkable. He was again on the ticket for coroner and among the successful candidates in November 1886.

people.name: Joe Pennell
people.role: Freighter; partner in Pennell & Roberts, Medora-Deadwood freight route promoter
people.bio: Joe "Doc" Pennell was a Medora freighter whose firm, Pennell & Roberts, joined the Marquis de Mores in early 1884 in pushing a freight and mail route from Medora to Deadwood and the Black Hills; the Marquis telegraphed asking him to organize post offices at ranches along the road. In February 1884 his firm lent its large room over the "Senate" for the stockmen's meeting. In April 1884 he and the Marquis set out from Medora at 4:30 a.m. hoping to cover the 185 miles to Deadwood in thirty-six hours; the trip took forty-eight. In late April he helped stake the route through the Bad Lands; in June the paper reported that Bob Roberts took out the first train ever to go over it, his and Pennell's. In July 1884 he helped decorate the hall for a ball and supper. From July 1884 the firm's mules did contract work on the Canadian Pacific, and by early 1885 the paper reported Pennell in the East, in charge of aqueduct work in New York for the Jones & Pennell outfit.

people.name: Peter J. Book
people.role: Mandan mason who opened Medora's brickyard and built its brick buildings
people.bio: Peter J. Book was a Mandan mason and contractor, known for building the People's block there, who tested Medora's butte clay in April 1884 and moved his family and five brick-makers to a yard south of town that month. He opened his first kiln in late May, was making pressed brick by June, and in August 1884 the Marquis gave him the contract for two brick cottages and asked him to plan a brick church. Over the winter he drew the brick plans for George Fitzgerald's new hotel and took the whole contract, and in March 1885 he also won the contract for an 85-foot slaughter-house smoke stack; the hotel was finished in May 1885. He was also a regular in the Bad Lands Gun Club shoots, and the paper mentioned "Pete Book's coal mine" up the river. In June 1885 he patented a lignite-burning brick kiln, and that summer he and most of his brick men worked on new buildings in Miles City, returning to Medora in September when the work there was done.

people.name: George W. Fitzgerald
people.role: Keeper of the Hotel de Mores; builder of a new Medora hotel
people.bio: George Fitzgerald kept the Hotel de Mores in Medora, where in 1884 he gave dances, lent his room to the April Republican convention, hosted a Catholic mass in August, and served as treasurer of the Little Missouri school fund. In July 1884 his appearance scared off three strangers who seemed ready to steal horses tied outside the hotel. From late 1884 he built a new hotel, with brick plans drawn by Peter Book and Henry Brick; the plastering and inside work were done by February 1885, and in April 1886 the paper said he meant to open it soon. In 1885 he was subpoenaed as a witness in William Roberts' horse-theft case at Miles City, and in December he settled a case against Gregor Lang when Lang bought his brand.

people.name: Gilbert A. Pierce
people.bio: Gilbert A. Pierce of Chicago was appointed governor of Dakota Territory in July 1884, replacing Ordway, and was welcomed at Bismarck that August by a crowd of over 2,000. In March 1885 he vetoed the bill to move the capital from Bismarck to Pierre, and the paper praised the veto's legal reasoning. Through 1885 the Cow Boy followed efforts to remove him and backed him, while Medora waited on his ruling on Billings County's petition for organization. He set Arbor Day in 1885 and issued Thanksgiving proclamations in 1885 and 1886, his name appeared on the 1886 notices of the Billings County election, and in October 1886 he proclaimed a quarantine against cattle from Chicago and Illinois because of pleuro-pneumonia. In December 1886 the paper reported that he had declined to serve past January and would return to journalism.

people.name: Lloyd Roberts
people.role: Pioneer cattleman and cattle buyer, Sloping Bottom ranch
people.bio: The Cow Boy introduced Lloyd Roberts in February 1884 as a pioneer cattleman who had driven the first herd into Bismarck, Standing Rock and the Bad Lands, and friends gave a dance in his honor at the Hotel de Mores. His ranch lay twelve miles up the river, later called the Sloping Bottom ranch. Each year he went east, usually to St. Cloud, Minn., with Daniel Friedman and others, to buy cattle for delivery to local ranchers and to buyers at Glendive; in June 1884 he and Howard Eaton brought in a thousand head for the Badger cattle company. In late August 1884 he and two others killed three buffalo from a herd south of town, and in October 1885 he finished grading for the new stock yards and took purchased buffalo to Rapid City. In 1886 he delivered a herd for Aleck Connell's Cave Hills ranch and spent the fall buying stock in St. Cloud and Cheyenne.

people.bio: Dorr Clark owned the VVV outfit and half of the E6 brand, and was listed as manager of Clark & Plum, with an office at 110 Dearborn Street, Chicago. people.name: William H. Merrifield
people.role: Partner in Ferris & Merrifield, managers of Roosevelt's Maltese Cross ranch
people.bio: William H. (Bill) Merrifield was a partner in Ferris & Merrifield, managers of the Maltese Cross (Chimney Butte) ranch seven miles up the Little Missouri from Medora. In March 1884 he sat on the committee that drafted by-laws for the Bad Lands stockmen's association. In June 1884 the paper noted that Theodore Roosevelt, the future president, then a New York assemblyman, was staying at Ferris & Merrifield's ranch, and that summer the firm shipped in a thousand head of cattle; Merrifield went east to buy more in March 1885 and brought back Elkhorn and Chimney Butte cattle that May. He and the Ferris brothers hosted dances and parties at the ranch, including a Thanksgiving dance in 1885. In January 1886 he and Sylvane Ferris went to Chicago at Roosevelt's invitation, and a report that he had married on the trip was later retracted as a made-up story. In August and September 1886 he hunted with Roosevelt in the Bull River mountains for a white goat, and that October Roosevelt turned the Elkhorn brand over to Ferris & Merrifield before Merrifield shipped cattle to Chicago and went home to Canada for the winter.

people.name: Vic Smith
people.bio: Vic Smith was described by the Cow Boy in June 1884 as one of the best hunters, trappers and scouts of the West, who said settlers were getting too thick and talked of going to Alaska. He was still in the area that September, finding a better line for the stage road in September 1884 and giving a petrified mastodon knee joint to the Cow Boy office museum. That October Bob Roberts hired him to collect petrifactions and game for Dakota's exhibit at the New Orleans exposition, and he hunted with the Marquis de Mores, who gave him a rifle; in late 1884 he guided Count Rembielinski on a hunt that took sixty-five deer and antelope. He traveled east in early 1885 but gave up his trip to the New Orleans exposition, then went beaver hunting down the Missouri from the Poplar river, and in May 1885 he and his brother Frank said they would make Medora their home. In July 1885 he went with the Marquise de Mores' hunting party to the Big Horn country, where he was struck with mountain fever, and by January 1886 he and his brother Bill were performing fancy rifle shooting at a Milwaukee dime museum as "Yellowstone Vic" and "Montana Bill."

people.name: Medora de Morès
people.role: Wife of the Marquis de Morès; builder of Medora's Catholic church
people.bio: The Marquise de Morès, wife of the Marquis, arrived in Medora in April 1884 in the Marquis' private car and came and went with him through 1886. In September 1884 the corner-stone was laid for a Catholic church she was building in the town, which Father Martin blessed that November; Catholic residents publicly thanked her, and she offered the church as a school house. The paper announced the birth of her son in March 1885, and that June she started the machinery of the new abattoir. In summer 1885 she went on a hunting trip to the Big Horn country, where the paper credited her with killing several bears, and she made more hunting trips down the river in 1885 and 1886, including one with the Marquis in October 1886 that took mountain sheep, elk and antelope. In October 1885 she renewed her offer to pay a teacher's salary if the school board would open a school.

He returned in May 1885 and that June and July the Cow Boy ran his serial history of the Lost Cabin gold mines, as told to him by his uncle, Allen Hulburt. In late June 1885 he sold his restaurant to M. W. McDonald and left for Miles City to organize a search for the mines, and by early July he had bought the Commercial house hotel in Glendive.

Conductor Clark was laid off in June 1884 on charges the paper called trumped up, was back on the road in July, returned to duty again in February 1885, and in March 1885 the paper reported that Mingusville cowboys who had made him dance were out on bail.

Conductor Clark returned to duty

people.name: Dick Moore
people.role: De Morès associate indicted in the Luffsey killing

In 1886 he brought two Siberian bloodhounds from New York for the Marquis de Morès's bear hunts, went with the Marquis to Powder river, and in July married Lizzie Hannon in St. Paul.

Brought bloodhounds from New York for the Marquis
Married Lizzie Hannon in St. Paul

people.name: E. A. Williams
people.bio: E. A. Williams of Bismarck was nominated for the territorial House at the October 1884 convention and visited Medora in June 1885 with Neil Gilmour of the Bismarck land office. In 1886 he campaigned through Medora as a Republican candidate for the House and was elected that November.

Listed among the successful candidates

people.name: Edw. P. Drury
people.role: Deputy sheriff of Morton County, at Mandan
people.bio: Edw. P. (Ed) Drury of Mandan was deputy sheriff of Morton County and served the law in Medora before Billings County was organized. In 1885 he came with Prosecuting Attorney T. K. Long to collect liquor licenses, served an attachment on the Cantonment property, signed sheriff's notices for Sheriff George W. Harmon, and in February 1886 his arrival with the Stark County sheriff scattered young men who had fired six-shooters at a departing train.

Served an attachment on the Cantonment property

people.name: George Blankenberg
people.role: Billings County Republican central committee member
people.bio: George Blankenberg signed the call for the April 1884 Billings County Republican convention and was elected there to the county central committee, and in October 1884 he and Max Bass, as members of the county central committee, signed a notice protesting that the chairman had called conventions without consulting the committee. That month he was elected a delegate at a Billings County convention held at Belfield, which the Cow Boy questioned.

Elected delegate at disputed Belfield county convention

people.name: George Myers
people.bio: George Myers was a Chimney Butte cowboy to whom Theodore Roosevelt gave a silver-mounted saddle outfit in August 1885, and he rode the 1886 O'Fallon Creek round-up. In December 1886 he was arrested on a Montana Stockgrowers' Association warrant for shipping two steers claimed not to be his in a car of Maltese Cross cattle; the Cow Boy defended him at length and reported that Roosevelt would come back from Europe to testify for him.

Arrested on a cattle-shipping charge

people.name: Gustave Grisy
people.role: Mingusville cattleman; former partner of Pierre Wibaux
people.bio: Gustave Grisy was a cattleman and partner of Pierre Wibaux in Grisy & Wibaux, who in April 1884 praised the country and said his losses would fall under one percent; the partnership ended November 1, 1884, leaving Wibaux sole owner of the Royal Chambord ranch on Beaver Creek. Based at Mingusville, Montana, Grisy stayed active in stockmen's meetings into 1886, and that spring his sorrel horse won a race.

Proposed a committee for the Medora and Miles City meetings

people.name: J. E. Hample
people.role: Hide buyer for Oberne, Hosick & Co., Chicago
people.bio: J. E. Hample was the traveling agent of the Chicago hide and leather firm Oberne, Hosick & Co., and in March 1884 he bought the hides at the Medora abattoir for about $20,000. He was back in Medora in October 1885, and the paper later noted he had several times bought the company's hides.

people.name: John Weber
people.bio: John Weber filed a complaint at the Bismarck land office against John Peehn for abandoning a homestead entry on the SE¼ of section 20, township 140, range 99, in Billings County. The notice summoning both parties to a hearing on August 21, 1884, ran in the Cow Boy from July to September 1884.

Contest notice ran for the last time

people.name: L. H. Palmer
people.role: Deadwood businessman on the Medora-Black Hills route
people.bio: L. H. Palmer was a Deadwood businessman, described in June 1884 as owning considerable property there, who praised the Medora-Black Hills freight route; in July 1884 the Cow Boy named him among Hills freighters who called it the best route they had travelled. He served as secretary of the Republican county convention in August 1884 and of a second convention in September, and left to winter in the Hills that October.

moments.label: Arrived in Medora from Deadwood
Served as secretary of the Republican county convention

people.name: Martin
people.bio: The name Martin appears in the Cow Boy for several different men: one who tracked stolen horses in April 1884, the father-in-law who ran a doctor's drug store in Medora in late 1884, a Black Hills legislator who supported the 1885 fence law, a man who panned gold up the river with Keeler in 1885, and an editor of the Montana Democrat at Miles City in 1886. Nothing in the excerpts shows that any two of these are the same person.

moments.label: Druggist Martin took charge of the new drug store

people.name: Riley Brooks
people.role: Round-up rider for the Refrigerator Car Co.
people.bio: Riley Brooks rode for the Refrigerator Car Co. in 1886, representing it at the Hashknife camp and gathering cattle on Crooked Creek and Grand River. In August 1886 he rode about eighteen miles in fifty-five minutes to report that George Fraser had been killed by lightning, and in December the paper announced his marriage to Lilly Roberts, then retracted the report as untrue.

Paper retracted report of his marriage

people.bio: Under the bare name Roberts, the paper reports a partner in Pennell & Roberts, which in 1884 backed the Deadwood freight route, lent its room over the 'Senate' for a stockmen's meeting, and in February 1885 brought back mules used on Canadian Pacific contract work. A Roberts also proposed with Paddock to surface Medora's streets with scoria, rode with an April 1884 posse after horse thieves, and in December 1884 shot George Heywood in his saloon after Heywood came in armed to kill him.

Shot George Heywood, who came armed to his saloon

people.name: Sam Townsend
people.bio: Sam Townsend was a freighter who in October 1884 hauled 50,000 pounds from Medora to Deadwood in seven days, which the paper called the fastest time ever from the Northern Pacific. He took charge of another man's mule train in 1885 and hauled for the stage company, and by October 1885 he was grading on the Northwestern's branch from Chadron toward the Black Hills.

Grading the Northwestern branch from Chadron

people.name: Samuel Whitney
people.role: Medora settler, constable and hotel landlord
people.bio: Samuel (Sam) Whitney settled in Medora in April 1885, setting up house in Bob Roberts's building, and won second place in the fat men's race at that year's Fourth of July sports. He was elected a Billings County constable in November 1886 and that month was to take over a Medora hotel as landlord.

Elected Billings County constable

people.name: T. J. Sharkey
people.bio: T. J. Sharkey was the Northern Pacific's traveling auditor, who came through Belfield and Medora in 1884 and 1885 to inspect station and express accounts. In December 1885 he protested, with citizens, a proposed change in Maxwell's position.

Protested the proposed change in Maxwell's position

people.name: Tommy Smith
people.role: Cowpuncher on the E6 ranch and other outfits
people.bio: Tommy Smith rode as a cowpuncher for the E6 ranch in 1885, reporting in August that about 4,000 steers would be shipped from that range, and in early 1886 returned to the W L ranch on Powder river. In October 1886 he came in from a season's work on the trail and in the British Possessions, and that winter he was in Deadwood.

moments.label: Returned to the E6 ranch as a cowpuncher
Back from trail work in the British Possessions

people.name: W. F. Steele
people.bio: Col. W. F. Steele of Kidder County was nominated for the house at a legislative convention reported in October 1884, and in October 1886 was the Republican nominee for the legislature from Kidder County, visiting Medora to look after his campaign; the paper said he represented the 'bull-dozing qualities' of the ticket. In the November 1886 returns, the Democrat Greene was reported to have a majority of 500 over him.

Reported beaten by Democrat Greene

people.name: Bill Nye
people.role: Humorist whose pieces the Cow Boy reprinted
people.bio: Bill Nye, the nationally known humorist, appeared in the Cow Boy through reprinted sketches and sayings, including 'Broncho Sam' in February 1884. In 1886 the paper carried his comic pieces on cattle brands and on the danger of overstocking the range.

Reprinted his warning about overstocking the range

people.name: C. F. Brown
people.role: Partner in Coleman & Brown, Medora hotel
people.bio: C. F. Brown bought a lot in June 1884 to build a boarding house, and was a partner in Coleman & Brown, proprietors of the Medora hotel, until the firm dissolved in September 1884. In May 1885 a citizens' meeting appointed him to ask residents to clean up their premises.

Appointed to request a town cleanup

people.name: Chester A. Arthur
people.bio: Chester A. Arthur, the 21st president, was mentioned by the Cow Boy in 1884 as a leading contender for the Republican nomination, favored by many businessmen. Paper praised him at his death

people.name: Frank O'Donald

people.bio: Frank O'Donald (also spelled O'Donnell) was a hunter and companion of Luffsey, who was killed in 1883 by a party that included the Marquis de Mores. In 1885 the paper recounted his drunken threat in 1883 to shoot the Marquis over his fencing, and at the Marquis's September 1885 trial witnesses testified that O'Donald and Luffsey had threatened the Marquis and had bad reputations; in January 1886 O'Donald claimed a share of Luffsey's estate as his partner.

Claimed share of Luffsey's estate as partner

Received 119 votes in the county election

Lost his shack and belongings to fire

people.name: James G. Ramsey
people.role: Glendive live-stock broker and insurance agent
people.bio: James G. Ramsey was a Glendive live-stock broker who in 1885 advertised Iowa yearling steers and grade Hereford bulls and made a number of sales. In 1886 he advertised accident insurance for cowboys, and by August he was agent for a Chicago stock commission firm.

Reported as agent for a Chicago commission firm

people.name: James M. Cook

Took a position with the Walter A. Wood firm

Expected to take charge of company's Medora interests

people.name: John Arrington
people.role: Cave Hills rancher on the Medora-Deadwood stage road
people.bio: John Arrington had a ranch in the Cave Hills on the stage road, where Dr. Jorgens spent Thanksgiving 1884 and the arrival of a baby in the Arrington household was reported in January 1885. In June 1885 the round-up gathered all but four of his herd of 250, and the paper called his ranch as pretty a location as any in the country.

Round-up gathered nearly all his Cave Hills herd

people.name: John Creedon
people.role: Candidate for constable in Billings County, 1886

moments.label: Named for constable on the Stockmen's ticket
Named for constable on the Billings County ticket

people.name: John L. Sullivan

Knocked out Paddy Ryan in San Francisco

people.name: L. C. Hunt

Hunt, a recent law graduate of the University of Michigan, came to Medora in October 1885 to learn the cattle business, and at the end of January 1886 bought Frank Moore's interest in the KC ranch and became manager of the KC herd. In September 1886, while he and his brother Robert were loading KC cattle at Dickinson, they learned their father had died at Fort Union, New Mexico, where L. C. went to bury him.

Learned of his father's death while loading KC cattle

people.name: L. N. Cary
people.role: Mandan man of the firm Carpenter & Cary; legislative candidate in 1884
people.bio: L. N. Cary of Mandan, of the firm of Carpenter & Cary, was the Cow Boy's favored candidate for the territorial legislature in the summer of 1884, endorsed in several issues. Located the site of the Dode Straugh murder

people.name: Martin Timlin
people.bio: Martin Timlin signed the Medora Catholics' public thanks to the Marquise de Mores for building their church in December 1884, won the men's first prize at a skating contest in April 1885, and gave a wedding gift with Alice Morrison that August. In November 1886 a partnership he was in dissolved, and he kept the business at the old stand.

Took over the business when his partnership dissolved

people.name: Mary J. Kiefer

In 1886 the paper printed a sheriff's sale notice in a foreclosure suit by the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company against her and her husband for $1,327.53 on a mortgage.

moments.label: Returned to Medora with health restored
Named in a foreclosure sale notice

people.name: McNeave Nally
people.role: Former Medora resident; witness in the Luffsey murder case
people.bio: McNeave Nally was to run a mercantile business at Medora for Mr. Huggins in 1884 and later moved to Jamestown. In September 1885 he returned as a witness in the Luffsey murder case, testifying that he had served on the coroner's jury, and in July 1886 the paper reported the death of his father in County Mayo, Ireland.

moments.label: Testified about the coroner's jury in the Luffsey case
Father reported dead in County Mayo, Ireland

people.name: Moody
people.role: Cowboy and lariat artist (Moody and Sankey)

The most-reported was Moody of the cowboy pair Moody and Sankey, skilled with the lariat, who left in May 1884 with a touring show outfit of Crow men, cowboys and wild broncos and returned to Medora in August after an engagement with the Rocky Mountain show.

moments.label: Left with a touring Wild West outfit
Returned after Rocky Mountain show engagement

people.name: Norman Lebo
people.role: Candidate for justice of the peace, Billings County, 1886
people.bio: Norman Lebo was nominated for justice of the peace on the Billings County and stockmen's tickets in March 1886. He appears in the April 1886 election returns for justice alongside Gregor Lang and J. C. Copeland.

moments.label: Nominated for justice of the peace on the county ticket
Ran for justice of the peace in county election

people.name: Orrin Kinley
people.role: Worker on the Medora-Deadwood stage route
people.bio: Orrin "Nich" Kinley returned from Deadwood with Robert Roberts in February 1884 and in May 1884 wounded his foot when his revolver went off by accident. In November 1884 he was working on the Medora-Deadwood stage route, getting the line ready for winter.

Returned from readying the stage route for winter

people.name: Oscar S. Gifford
people.bio: Oscar S. Gifford was Dakota's delegate to Congress, and the paper followed his bid for renomination at the Republican convention in Yankton in September 1886. He was re-elected that November, and in December he offered a bill for a railroad bridge across the Missouri near Yankton.

moments.label: Re-elected delegate to Congress
Offered a bill for a Missouri bridge at Yankton

people.name: R. H. Montgomery
people.bio: R. H. (Bob) Montgomery was a Belfield man who visited Medora in February 1884 with good reports of his town and was sick that March. The Belfield columns of 1884 noted the redecoration of his place and a new addition to it, and his return from the east in August.

moments.label: Built an addition at Belfield
Returned to Belfield from the east

people.name: Samuel English
people.role: Medora dealer in fruits, fish and game
people.bio: Sam English came to Medora in April 1884 to go into business and was soon dealing in fruits, fish and game; in November 1884 the paper announced the birth of his daughter. By early April 1885 he and his wife had moved to Brainerd, where he was interested in land along a new railroad.

moments.label: Selling fish in his new fruit, fish and game business
Moved to Brainerd

people.name: Sitting Bull
people.role: Hunkpapa Lakota leader living at Standing Rock

In March 1886 the paper reported him at his camp near Standing Rock in poor health and said his voice no longer guided the Sioux.

moments.label: Reported target of an attempted horse theft
Reported in failing health near Standing Rock

people.name: T. J. Bryan
people.role: President of the Montana Stockgrowers' Association
people.bio: T. J. Bryan chaired the April 1885 Miles City meeting of the eastern Montana stockgrowers, remarking that two years earlier the association had had seven members and met in a little back room. As president of the Montana Stockgrowers' Association he passed through Medora in November 1885 on the way to the national association meeting.

moments.label: Chaired the stockgrowers' spring meeting
Passed through Medora to the national meeting

people.name: T. W. Ives
people.bio: T. W. Ives was the telegraph operator at Sentinel Butte, who came to Medora for the Thanksgiving ball in November 1884. Still operating the telegraph at Sentinel Butte

Sheriff Tuttle defeated Matthews at Glendive

people.name: W. H. Minty

Left for a Missouri Pacific office at Lincoln

people.name: Western Starr
people.role: Justice of the peace at Dickinson
people.bio: Western Starr was a justice of the peace at Dickinson who visited Medora on legal business and, in 1885-86, fined Medora men brought before him for firing weapons and for assault. At a Fourth of July celebration in 1886 he read the Declaration of Independence.

Read the Declaration of Independence on July Fourth

people.name: William Tolbert
people.role: Ran the Elk saloon in Little Missouri; later in the National Park country

Reported at the National Park stage line

people.name: Alex. Morton

people.name: Alexander Hughes

Alexander Hughes of Burleigh County was nominated for the Council at the October 1886 legislative convention in Bismarck, which the paper complained had ignored the west-Missouri country. moments.label: Nominated for the Council at Bismarck
Listed among the successful candidates

people.name: Allen Hulburt

Accused thieves brought through under arrest

Protested the change in agent Maxwell's position

people.name: E. E. Ball
people.role: Mandan dentist making visits to Medora
